newsitem.title: FRANCE: France submits Credit Lyonnais recovery plan to EU.
newsitem.headline: France submits Credit Lyonnais recovery plan to EU.

text.p: France's new Socialist government has submitted to the European Union a long-awaited restructuring plan for state bank Credit Lyonnais which does not aim for the quick sell-off sought by the previous government.

A Finance Ministry spokeswoman said privatisation was not the focus of the plan, which aims to win the European Commission's approval to neutralise the estimated three-billion franc ($500 million) cost of a loan Credit Lyonnais made to a state holding company.

"Privatisation is not the focus of the plan. There were promises made in 1995 in a five-year plan. They will be evaluated in due course in the best interests of Credit Lyonnais and its employees and the interests of the state," she said.
The previous centre-right government, ousted in a surprise election defeat in June, had pledged no more recapitalisations of the bank and a sale in late 1998 or early 1999.

Without the Commission's approval to neutralise the cost of the cheap loan to finance the spinoff of Lyonnais' bad assets into a separate holding company, the bank's performance would be badly hit, wiping out its expected 1997 net profit.
The spokeswoman said thanks to a recovery in the bank's performance, she did not expect any recapitalisations in the near future.
The government was confident in the future of Lyonnais and would do its job to save the bank and its employees, she said.
Credit Lyonnais has staged a strong recovery from an ill-fated expansion spree carried out when the Socialists were last in power, which nearly resulted in its collapse.
It is expected to post a 1997 net profit of around 1.5 billion francs.
The final tally of its misadventures, which led to a series of state bailouts, is seen at around 170 billion francs.
The new plan submitted by Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn focuses on improving the profitability of the bank and the disposal of Lyonnais' retail banking network outside France.

"This plan, prepared by Credit Lyonnais, aims to ease the way to its recovery by increasing its profitibility...The improvement in profitability is a determining factor in enabling changes in the bank," the finance ministry said in a statement.

"As regards its international strategy, the plan envisages continued concentration of Credit Lyonnais' activity on large businesses and institutions, private fund management and financial markets," it said. "Credit Lyonnais will largely free itself from its retail banking activity outside France."

After selling its Dutch subsidiary and putting its 54 percent stake in Irish financial services group Woodchester Investments Plc up for sale, Lyonnais sold its 56.8 percent stake in Italian bank Credito Bergamasco earlier this week. ($ = 6.184 French Francs)
